newsitem.title: USA: U.S. gas, power prices up sharply on forecast cold.
newsitem.headline: U.S. gas, power prices up sharply on forecast cold.

text.p: A cold front bearing down on the central U.S. and Gulf Coast continued to push natural gas and electricity prices sharply higher on Monday as the region braces for an early taste of winter.

The scramble for natgas supplies sent gas prices on the Gulf Coast pipelines for November 1 delivery soaring to $2.80 per million British thermal units (mmBtu) Monday, up 80 to 90 cents from October 1 levels.
"There are a lot of people short. It will definitely go up before it goes down," said one natural gas trader.
Forecasters said the cold air is expected to hit the nation's midsection at the end of the week.
Along the southern Texas coast, buyers were forced to pay about $2.60 for gas to begin flowing on November 1, as compared to the low-$1.70s evident during October midweek.

Following the lead of natural gas, a key fuel in power generation, peak firm electricity prices at the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) pool for Tuesday jumped to about $28.00 per megawatt hour (MWh) from Friday's $23.00-24.50 range.
November pricing ranged from about $22.50 to $23.30, up more than a $1 from Friday's levels.

In the Northwest, where early wintry weather already has taken its toll on energy supplies and gas users continue to deplete storage caverns, gas prices at Sumas, Wash., a Canadian export point, surged to about $2.40 per mmBtu for November, compared with just under $1 only a month ago.
These inflated prices are consistent with the normally constrained Rocky Mountain market in the $2.50s, up from the high-$1.20s on October 1 and the $1.18 area on September 1.
The squeeze in supplies has also reached down into southern California, where gas prices jumped into the $2.70s for November 1, up about $1 from October 1.
Traders there were citing the below-normal storage inventories (about 70 percent full) as one factor pushing the market higher.

As buyers scramble for additional energy supplies, next-day prices for peak, firm power at the California-Oregon border (COB) have risen an average of $4 in one month. Prices at COB were talked around $21.50-24.50 per MWh area today.

The inflated price rally has not been reserved for only the western U.S. Despite expectations for normal temperatures in the early part of November, gas prices at the New York city-gate for next month delivery are up an average of $1.25 in the $3.30-3.50 area.
In the Pennsylvania-New Jersey-Maryland (PJM) Interconnect pool, peak, firm electricity prices for November are in the $23.45-23.60 range, compared with month-ago levels of about $18.50 per MWh.
